exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 17–24, $$A$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix with a singular value decomposition $$A = U \text{Σ} V^{T}$$ , where $$U$$ is an $$m \times m$$ orthogonal matrix, $$\text{Σ}$$ is an $$m \times n$$ “diagonal” matrix with $$r$$ positive entries and no negative entries, and $$V$$ is an $$n \times n$$ orthogonal matrix. Justify each answer.

problem.paragraph: Show that if $$A$$ is square, then $$|\det A|$$ is the product of the singular values of $$A$$ .
Suppose $$A$$ is square and invertible. Find a singular value decomposition of $$A^{- 1}$$ .

Show that the columns of $$V$$ are eigenvectors of $$A^{T}A$$ , the columns of $$U$$ are eigenvectors of $$AA^{T}$$ , and the diagonal entries of $$\text{Σ}$$ are the singular values of $$A$$ . [Hint: Use the SVD to compute $$A^{T}A$$ and $$AA^{T}$$ .]
Show that if $$P$$ is an orthogonal $$m \times m$$ matrix, then $$PA$$ has the same singular values as $$A$$ .

Justify the statement in Example 2 that the second singular value of a matrix $$A$$ is the maximum of $$\parallel A\textbf{x} \parallel$$ as $$\textbf{x}$$ varies over all unit vectors orthogonal to $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , with $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ a right singular vector corresponding to the first singular value of $$A$$ . [Hint: Use Theorem 7 in Section 7.3.]
Show that if $$A$$ is an $$n \times n$$ positive definite matrix, then an orthogonal diagonalization $$A = {PDP}^{T}$$ is a singular value decomposition of $$A$$ .

Let $$U = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{lll} \textbf{u}_{1} & \cdots & \textbf{u}_{m} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$V = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{lll} \textbf{v}_{1} & \cdots & \textbf{v}_{n} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , where the $$\textbf{u}_{i}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{i}$$ are as in Theorem 10. Show that $$A = \sigma_{1} \textbf{u}_{1} \textbf{v}_{1}^{T} + \sigma_{2} \textbf{u}_{2} \textbf{v}_{2}^{T} + \hdots + \sigma_{r} \textbf{u}_{r} \textbf{v}_{r}^{T}$$
Using the notation of Exercise 23, show that $$A^{T}\textbf{u}_{j} = \sigma_{j}\textbf{v}_{j}$$ for $$1 \leq j \leq r = \text{rank} A$$ .

Let $$T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ be a linear transformation. Describe how to find a basis $$B$$ for $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and a basis $$C$$ for $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ such that the matrix for $$T$$ relative to $$B$$ and $$C$$ is an $$m \times n$$ “diagonal” matrix.

problem.paragraph: [T] Compute the singular values of the $$4 \times 4$$ matrix in Exercise 9 in Section 2.3, and compute the condition number $$\sigma_{1}/\sigma_{4}$$ .
[T] Compute the singular values of the $$5 \times 5$$ matrix in Exercise 10 in Section 2.3, and compute the condition number $$\sigma_{1}/\sigma_{5}$$ .

If $$A = U \text{Σ} V^{T}$$ , where $$\text{Σ}$$ is $$m \times n$$ , then $$A^{T} = (V^{T})^{T} \text{Σ} ^{T}U^{T} = V \text{Σ} ^{T}U^{T}$$ . This is an SVD of $$A^{T}$$ because $$V$$ and $$U$$ are orthogonal matrices and $$\text{Σ} ^{T}$$ is an $$n \times m$$ “diagonal” matrix. Since $$\text{Σ}$$ and $$\text{Σ} ^{T}$$ have the same nonzero diagonal entries, $$A$$ and $$A^{T}$$ have the same nonzero singular values. [Note: If $$A$$ is $$2 \times n$$ , then $$AA^{T}$$ is only $$2 \times 2$$ and its eigenvalues may be easier to compute (by hand) than the eigenvalues of $$A^{T}A$$ .]

Use the SVD to write $$A = U \text{Σ} V^{T}$$ , where $$U$$ and $$V$$ are $$n \times n$$ orthogonal matrices and $$\text{Σ}$$ is an $$n \times n$$ diagonal matrix. Notice that $$U^{T}U = I = V^{T}V$$ and $$\text{Σ} ^{T} = \text{Σ}$$ , since $$U$$ and $$V$$ are orthogonal matrices and $$\text{Σ}$$ is a diagonal matrix. Substituting the SVD for $$A$$ into $$AA^{T}$$ and $$A^{T} A$$ results in $$A A^{T} = U \Sigma V^{T} \left(\right. U \Sigma V^{T} \left.\right)^{T} = U \Sigma V^{T} V \Sigma^{T} U^{T} = U \Sigma\Sigma^{T} U^{T} = U \Sigma^{2} U^{T} ,$$
and $$A^{T} A = \left(\right. U \Sigma V^{T} \left.\right)^{T} U \Sigma V^{T} = V \Sigma^{T} U^{T} U \Sigma V^{T} = V \Sigma^{T} \Sigma V^{T} = V \Sigma^{2} V^{T} .$$
Let $$Q = VU^{T}$$ . Then $$Q^{T} ( A^{T} A ) Q = \left(( V U^{T} )\right)^{T} ( V \Sigma^{2} V^{T} )( V U^{T} ) & = U V^{T} V \Sigma^{2} V^{T} V U^{T} & = U \Sigma^{2} U^{T} = A A^{T} .$$
